pitch_detail.notes: Climb a ribbon of ice on the initial slabs, reached through a break in the lower cliffs right of the steepest part of the headwall. On the first ascent it was about 65°, half an inch to an inch thick and too thin for protection or belays. It thinned to 5.8 mixed moves on edges, then a short near-vertical step on a thicker tongue, then more thin 65° ice to the bowl.

Low-angle snow crosses the bowl toward the couloir, which cuts through shale bands several gullies right of the north rib. The bowl steepens to about 35° on the avalanche fan below the couloir. Snow ranges from névé to wind crust over powder, and rockfall and slides come down this fan, so do not linger.

The first of three steeper steps in the couloir: about two pitches of névé and water ice at roughly 75°, narrowing in one place to a slot about three feet wide with fat ice at the back. Protection is available here. About 300 ft of steeper ground in all brings you to the top of the step.

Rotten shale, snow mushrooms and thin, strange ice. It starts on good 75° ice, then the ice gives out to powder over shale and the picks have to be dragged through snow until they catch. Protection and belay options are very poor, and the angle drops to about 60° on thicker ice at the top.

At about three-quarters height, the third and steepest step. In good conditions it is a near-vertical ice pitch leading to steep, often runnelled snow. In lean conditions it has gone as rotten ice over shale at 80–95°, with drytooling and a knifeblade in a shale seam as the main protection. The belay at its base is poor.

About 1,000 ft of mostly névé and ice remains above the third step and can be simul-climbed with occasional screws. In the last few hundred feet the snow can turn unconsolidated and give no protection, which makes this exposed upper slope one of the most serious parts of the route. A short mixed section sits just below the cornices.

Summit cornices can overhang the face by about six feet. The first ascent cut a tunnel through them with an adze to reach the ridge. The route finishes on the summit ridge, well to the west of the true summit, where a boulder offers a solid cam anchor for bringing up the second.

Start right of the Northeast Couloir, at the foot of the Hidden Couloir. Two rope-stretching pitches of ice lead into the couloir. They take screws well when formed, and grades given range from AI3 to AI3+. This is the most reliable ice on the route; the ground above depends on winter snow conditions.

Start right of the Northeast Couloir, at the foot of the Hidden Couloir. Two rope-stretching pitches of ice lead into the couloir. They take screws well when formed, and grades given range from AI3 to AI3+. This is the most reliable ice on the route; the ground above depends on winter snow conditions.
Leave the Hidden Couloir and climb a few hundred feet of 50–60° snow up and left toward a steep rock band. Protection is sparse, so carry a picket, and the slope loads with wind-drifted snow.

Two pitches of unconsolidated snow over moderate rock. Clear the snow to find placements for rock gear and pins, and move carefully: the snow gives little hold for tools, and a slip here runs down the slope below.
Traverse about 30 ft left into a chimney and climb two pitches of M6 mixed ground up it. Stubby screws, pitons and small cams protect it. This is the sustained technical heart of the route.
More steep snow leads to a final rock band. Climb through it to a notch on the north ridge crest.
Out of the north-ridge notch, a tricky wide crack at M6 is the last hard move. From its top, traverse around to the west into the final couloir of the North Buttress Couloir route.
Up the final couloir of the North Buttress Couloir line, one more short but steep mixed pitch reaches the summit, which is often rimed and windswept in winter. Descend by the Colchuck Glacier.
Agnes Creek Trail/PCT, ~8-9 mi, 1,700-2,800 ft; maintained trail via Fivemile Camp (2,200 ft, ~5-5.5 mi)
pitch_detail.pitch: High Bridge to Swamp Creek Camp

pitch_detail.notes: Off-trail on the abandoned Swamp Creek climbers' path; log crossing of Swamp Creek, ~0.25 mi of heavy brush, hard to follow
pitch_detail.pitch: Swamp Creek Camp to lower basin

pitch_detail.notes: Cross-country, roughly 4-5 hours of further travel
pitch_detail.pitch: Lower basin to upper basin (~4,300 ft)

pitch_detail.notes: ~3,000 ft of steep terrain, often snow, no established track; alternatively reached via ~3,500 ft of open-forest climbing from Hemlock Camp on the PCT variant
pitch_detail.pitch: Upper basin to Dark Fin Col

pitch_detail.notes: Crevassed; right side of the glacier reported as the better line; travel from roughly 7,000 ft to 8,250 ft
Technical crux; exits the glacier onto rock at the top
Short rock scramble to the true summit

Leave the Boston Glacier across the moat or bergschrund at the face's margin, which widens through the season, and climb the rock just below and to the left of the large ice patch on the lower face. The section is rated old-style grade III and was first protected with a few pitons; expect no fixed gear, and treat this outline with caution because the face sees very few ascents.

The technical centre of the route: a sustained ice patch at about 50°. It faces north and has thinned across the range since the first ascent, so check that it still holds enough ice for screws before committing. Everything on the upper face drains through this patch, making it the place most exposed to falling rock and ice from above.

Above the ice the face stays steep, but the rock is stacked in upward-dipping slabs that give holds and make it easier than it appears from below; it leads directly to the summit. Do not plan to reverse the face: the descent is by another route, and Forbidden has no easy way off by any line.
From the SW buttress base, ascend snow slopes toward the first bergschrund.
Cross a snow bridge and climb directly up the face of a ~50-ft serac.
Two roped 60m pitches through narrow gullies with runnel crossings.
Knife-edge arete requiring careful tool and crampon placement.
Final ~20 ft of scrambling on loose rock past crumbling rime-ice features to the summit.

From High Camp near 6,900–7,100 ft, climb the moraine and snow gully to the toe of the Adams Glacier and rope up. The lower glacier is moderate walking that steepens around 8,500 ft. Hold toward the right (west) third of the glacier from the start: the eastern flank carries an active icefall that has dropped multiple large seracs in a single afternoon.

Between about 9,200 and 11,800 ft the glacier pours through a steep icefall of seracs and crevasses. Low in it, expect a series of ice steps around 45°, each about a rope length, mixing steep snow, crumbly ice and hard glacial ice; most parties belay or run protection on pickets and screws. The line changes year to year and through the season.

The steepest ground, typically a 45° ice slope of about two pitches around 9,500–10,200 ft, followed by large crevasses that can force long lateral traverses to find a crossing. Some years a bridgeless crack must be rappelled into and climbed out of. Reported grades run AI2 to AI3. Stay out from under the seracs and keep moving.

Pass the upper icefall on whichever side the crevasses allow, working left onto easier névé that leads to the false-summit plateau. From there it is a long, gentle traverse across the summit plateau to the true summit at 12,276 ft. Top out early; the icefall below gets more active as the day warms.

pitch_detail.grade: Hiking, mix of forest and meadow terrain
pitch_detail.notes: Multiple creek crossings, persistent snow late June/early July crosses the trail, ice axe recommended early season for icy sections
pitch_detail.pitch: 1-2: Approach via Thunder Creek Trail to Park Creek Pass

pitch_detail.notes: Gently rising traverse across high alpine, crosses rib at 7,600 ft, steep gully passage through cliff bands around 7,350 ft with possible snow/ice
Gentle glacier traverse, roped team recommended, crevasses generally small and avoidable but present
Steeper glacier leading to south ridge (Hogsback), moat crossing to access ridge crest, late-season snow bridge may be absent

Approximately 300 vertical feet of scrambling, cross Hogsback notch, descend briefly then traverse ledges on east side of summit ridge, final 100 feet Class 3-4 with good holds and solid rock, some exposure
pitch_detail.pitch: 6: Summit scramble via Hogsback and east side

pitch_detail.notes: From the notch above Ice Lakes, rope up and descend onto the Entiat Glacier, then find a short way across the ablation zone of the shrinking glacier. The crossing is trickier than older photos suggest. Skirt below the rock spur and head up toward the icefall.

Work rightward beneath the headwall through big crevasses, climbing short vertical ice steps and ramps between them; most parties move on a running belay with screws and a picket. In a big snow year steep snow slopes to one side can bypass part of the ice. The icefall has shrunk greatly and its shape changes from year to year.

Above the crevasses, gentler slopes of ice and snow at around 35° lead to the base of the rock. The rock above is slower than it looks from here; allow several hours for it rather than a quick scramble.

Turn right off the ice onto the rock, where several ramps offer a start. The rock is crumbly and protection is scarce, so running belays are the usual method. Take the line of least resistance, trending slightly toward the ridge crest.

Continue on loose fourth and low-fifth-class ground toward the crest; the rock section totals roughly 900 vertical feet and commonly takes several hours. Near the top there is a step-across at the head of a couloir. Test holds before weighting them; rockfall onto the party below is the main hazard.
A short walk leads to the heavily cairned 9,082 ft summit. Descend the South Ridge on foot, which is quick in good conditions and returns toward the Ice Lakes bivy ledges.

Drop off Curtis Ridge onto the Carbon Glacier at about 7,300 ft and cross to the toe of the ridge near 8,600 ft. In May and June several lines usually go; later the glacier breaks up. The usual crux is the moat between glacier and ridge, which has turned strong parties back. The ridge can be gained from either flank or directly at the toe.

The crest proper from the toe has loose rocky steps and uneven climbing; a flank gives steadier snow but sits under rockfall. The east flank is steeper with more rock bands, so parties starting there cross over the crest to the west side and continue to Thumb Rock, the obvious gendarme near 10,500 ft. Rocks come down without warning here, so climb it early in the day.

The small saddle just above Thumb Rock is the only real bivouac on the ridge, limited to twelve people. Dig platforms and build a wall against wind and the small rocks that fall from the cliff above. Above this point no safe bivy exists, and retreat grows harder than continuing up, so settle the weather forecast and team condition here.

Above camp a rock band (the Gun Sight) blocks the crest. The easiest line goes out left (east) around it and up the east side of the ridge; when it is formed, a short water-ice pitch goes straight through the middle. The right-hand bypass crosses under loose rock and is the poorest choice. Rockfall off the Gun Sight has triggered a very large slab avalanche on the slope below.

Climb up and left to pass the Black Pyramid, a dark rock buttress over 1,000 ft tall, on its left (east) side from about 11,800 to 12,800 ft. The ground is steep snow or low-angle alpine ice depending on the season, on exposed faces reported up to 60°. Screws and pickets for running protection; regain the rounded crest above the Pyramid at 12,800 ft.

The bergschrund near 13,800 ft is the last and usually hardest obstacle. In some years it is a step over a small crack and a snow ramp; in others an offset gap with a thin, awkward bridge and a near-vertical wall above. Anchor the belayer and pitch it out when it is dicey, and belay out of the fall line, since sun-baked or wind-hammered ice here breaks off in large plates.

Above the schrund, slopes ease to Liberty Cap at about 14,110 ft; fast or grinding depending on the surface. Columbia Crest is over a mile away: most parties drop about 600 ft to Liberty Saddle to join the Emmons-Winthrop descent, and the Crest adds about 800 ft of climbing from the saddle. Stay roped through the saddle, where crevasses are thinly bridged and cornices form on its east side.

From the high camp at about 10,200–10,300 ft below the Ptarmigan ice cliffs, descend onto the Mowich Glacier to the bergschrund at about 9,800 ft, crossing avalanche-prone slopes on the way. The usual crossing is a snow bridge just left of a rock outcrop near the middle of the face.

Above the schrund make a rising traverse back east toward the ice cliffs, threading an obvious passage through the rock bands on about 1,000 ft of 40–45° snow. Staying close under the cliffs on the right keeps the route-finding simple as far as the hourglass. Lower-face snow can be rotten and unsupportive once it warms.

At a steep rock band traverse left into the hourglass-shaped snow face and climb it on either side to the base of the big rock buttress that splits the upper route (~11,500 ft). Exposed; protect with pickets and screws, and belay if rockfall is active. At the buttress the 1935 line goes left and contours onto the slopes between the buttress and the icefall (45–55°, often icy); most parties now go right.

From the toe of the buttress climb a short way to the final ice slope, typically several hundred feet of blue ice around 55°, then cross a rock rib and traverse snow or ice to the exit chute, the first major break in the ridge's cliffs. The chute is easy 5th class with a near-vertical step that may hold a fixed pin or two; rock is fractured, so bring screws plus a light rock rack and pins.
pitch_detail.pitch: Right variation: ice slope and exit chute

pitch_detail.notes: Above the chute, easier scrambling leads onto the Liberty Cap Glacier. Climb about 1,000 ft of glacier slopes, cut back right to the ridge crest through the crevasse pattern, and follow easy slopes along the crest to Liberty Cap (~14,110 ft). Good bivy sites exist on the lower Liberty Cap Glacier. Surface conditions decide whether this is quick or a grind.
pitch_detail.pitch: Liberty Cap Glacier to Liberty Cap

pitch_detail.notes: Columbia Crest is more than a mile away: drop about 600 ft into Liberty Saddle and climb about 800 ft back up to the summit. Stay roped, since crevasses between Liberty Cap and the crest can be thinly bridged and deep, and large cornices form on the east side of the saddle. The descent via the Emmons–Winthrop leaves from the saddle.

The face is the headwall of the Carbon Glacier's eastern cirque, between Liberty Ridge and Curtis Ridge. The lower lines start from the upper Carbon Glacier, reached up the glacier from the Carbon River side or across it from a camp near the foot of Liberty Ridge (about 8,600 ft). Some upper-wall link-ups instead come in from the White River side, over St. Elmo Pass and the Winthrop Glacier to a high camp on Curtis Ridge, then traverse onto the face.

A very large bergschrund guards the foot of the wall. Above it, three ribs (West, Central and East) give the only relief from the avalanche and rockfall paths between them. Expect steep snow faces around 45° broken by rock bands and small buttresses. The Central Rib carries the most rockfall, and all but the westernmost line sit under active seracs.

Higher up, the ribs give way to mixed rock and ice, then ice steps of 50–60°, beneath a 200–300 ft ice cliff that caps the whole face and sheds ice onto the lines below. A crevasse can run the width of the ice cap here. Lines either climb through the cliff to the summit plateau near Liberty Cap, or traverse beneath it (the Traverse of the Angels) to exit onto Liberty Ridge or Curtis Ridge.

From the bivy at about 5,500 ft, where the ridge meets the face, traverse left across the base through the lower glacier's cracks. The first few hundred feet hold the largest crevasses; trend climber's right of the main runnel to stay out from under icefall off the Hanging Glacier. Late season, a schrund can block the direct start; a left-leaning snow gully gets around it.

Climb the long, continuous face on snow and runnels at about 45 degrees. Near 6,900 ft the line passes through a notch between two rock outcrops, and above it there is less cliff on either side. The upper face gets little early sun and stays firmer. In good snow it is often climbed unroped; late season it turns icy and a second tool and ice screws are needed.

The face steepens to about 50 degrees just below the exit, then tops out onto the broad shoulder between the Crystal and Hanging Glaciers, around 8,400 ft and northeast of the summit pyramid. On firm snow this is the most sustained ground of the route, with the whole face below.

From the shoulder, traverse the ice plateau around the east side of the summit pyramid to its south face, then finish up the central gully of the standard route (mostly 3rd-4th class with a few harder moves). The usual descent is the White Salmon Glacier back toward the cars, not the face.

From the camps near 5,400 ft in the upper Mountaineer Creek basin, gain the moraine and follow it up toward the toe of the North Ridge at about 6,600 ft. The moraine is loose; in early season most of it is snow-covered and quick. Rope up and gear up before leaving the moraine, because the next stage runs beneath the ice cliff.

Cut hard left from the base of the North Ridge and traverse beneath the ice cliff toward whichever flank of the icefall will be climbed. The slope is littered with avalanche debris and blocks of glacier ice that have fallen from the cliff above. Move through quickly and do not stop to rest under the cliff.

Pass the icefall on one flank. In early season the left side gives a snowy couloir with short steps of steep ice, AI2 to AI3 depending on conditions, then a traverse right over the lip onto flatter glacier. Late in the season the ice recedes and a 5.8 slab on the right side is often the better option. Screws are needed on the ice steps; bring a small rock rack late season.

Above the icefall, take the line of least resistance across the cirque toward the base of the upper couloir. Crevasses open here as the season advances, and fresh snow on the plateau can be deep and slow. Cross the bergschrund on the right side of the couloir's foot.

Climb roughly 1,000 ft of sustained couloir, staying near its left side, and take the right-hand fork near the top. In fat conditions it is steep snow; in lean conditions or late season it turns to hard snow-ice and blue ice up to 60–70°, and then needs screws and careful front-pointing. Pickets protect the snow sections. Rock and ice fall down the couloir once the sun reaches the face.

The couloir exits through a cornice onto the south-facing ridge just below the false summit at about 8,600 ft. When the cornice is large this is the hardest part of the climb: loose, near-vertical snow needing careful tool work. Look right for a smaller break before tunnelling or climbing the steepest section.

From the exit, traverse below the false summit on its south side, then follow the summit ridge past rime-covered spires to the true summit (9,415 ft). The ridge can hold snow and rime well into the season. Descend by the Sherpa Glacier or the Cascadian Couloir; do not reverse the ice route.

Start from the upper SE corner of the Lower Curtis Glacier, on the snow slope below the obvious glacier tongue that reaches halfway up the face, aiming for the narrow gully at the right side of the main wall. The slope steepens to about 45° near its top and ends at a large transverse crevasse, crossed on a snow bridge; check the bridge before committing.

Above the crevasse a short band of vertical ice forms in an open-book rock corner, climbed as an ice-filled chimney in its middle, followed immediately by a second, shorter vertical step. This is the steepest ice on the route; carry a tool as well as an axe and a couple of screws.
Steep snow continues above the ice chimney to the top of the icefall. Stay in the gully line on the right side of the wall; the rock step that follows is the only way onto the glacier tongue above.

A short band of easy fifth-class rock with no protection leads from the top of the icefall onto the narrow glacier tongue. Climb it with care, likely in crampons; with no gear, a slip here would run back down the icefall.
Steep snow on the tongue leads to a second large transverse crevasse. It crosses easily on its left end; do not try to force it in the middle.

The steepest sustained ground of the lower route: ice that starts around 60° and steepens to about 70° near the top, turning to snow before the base of the rock headwall. Pickets and screws both have a place here depending on how much snow covers the ice.

At the base of the headwall traverse left to a less-than-vertical weakness and climb it on fourth-class rock to a ledge. From the ledge traverse left around a corner to reach the foot of the long buttress.

A long buttress of easy fifth-class climbing on good, solid rock with positive holds, climbed for roughly its whole height to the crest of the main SE Ridge south of the Hourglass. A minimal rack of nuts and extra-long slings covers it.
Drop off the east side of the rocky SE Ridge crest onto the Sulphide Glacier and follow it north to the south side of the summit pyramid. Rope up for the glacier; it is crevassed.

Climb the summit pyramid by the regular fourth-class line, or take a direct line of roughly 800 ft of easy fifth-class rock. In low visibility on the way down, stay high and traverse directly below the Hourglass to avoid the Upper Curtis icefall.
Barclay Lake Trail to a Barclay/Tailgunner Creek bushwhack and an overgrown logging road up to about 4,000 ft.
Scramble crossing of a waterfall ravine around 4,000 ft.
Grass and snow patches leading to Tailgunner Pass (roughly 5,320-5,360 ft).
Series of steep snow faces and rock benches; crampons and running belays used on hard/refrozen snow.
Horribly exposed snowfinger below the summit horn; often protected with a picket and belayed or roped.
Final short rock section to the true summit; rappelled on descent.
